title: What test-design techniques do you apply to reduce case count while keeping coverage (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables, state transition testing, pairwise/combinatorial), and how do they help you choose which inputs to test?
shortTitle: Test-design techniques to reduce case count while keeping coverage
keyPoints: Equivalence partitioning groups inputs into classes the system treats the same, so one representative per class suffices
Boundary value analysis tests the edges of each partition where off-by-one bugs and wrong comparison operators cluster
Decision tables enumerate condition combinations and expected actions, exposing missing or contradictory specification rules
State transition testing covers an entity's lifecycle states and both legal and illegal transitions between them
Pairwise testing covers all value pairs with far fewer cases than the full cross-product, catching most combination defects
These techniques are complementary: partition to shrink, boundary to find edge bugs, table for logic, state for lifecycle, pairwise for explosion

s1_definition.oneliner: Equivalence partitioning picks one input per class, boundary value analysis tests the edges, decision tables cover condition combinations, state transition testing covers legal and illegal moves, and pairwise testing covers all value pairs, so you get strong coverage with few cases and can justify every one.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Equivalence partitioning** – Groups inputs into classes the system treats the same, so one representative per class gives the same confidence as testing every member.
- **Boundary value analysis** – Tests the exact edges of each partition where off-by-one errors and wrong comparison operators cluster.
- **Decision tables** – Enumerates combinations of conditions and their expected actions, exposing missing or contradictory rules in the specification.
- **State transition testing** – Models an entity's lifecycle states and covers each legal transition plus attempts at illegal ones.
- **Pairwise testing** – Covers all pairs of parameter values with far fewer cases than the full cross-product, because most defects are triggered by two-parameter interactions.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India accepts transfer amounts from one rupee to one hundred thousand rupees. Testing every single amount is impossible, so a smart tester groups amounts into "too low," "valid," and "too high" and tests one from each group; that is equivalence partitioning. Then the tester checks the exact edges, zero, one, one hundred thousand, one hundred thousand and one; that is boundary value analysis. When loan approval depends on several yes-or-no conditions, the tester lays out all the combinations in a grid; that is a decision table. When a loan moves through applied, approved, disbursed, and closed, the tester checks every allowed and forbidden move; that is state transition testing. And when a form has many dropdowns, the tester covers every pair of choices instead of every combination; that is pairwise testing.

```text
  Equivalence Partitioning + Boundary Value Analysis
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Transfer Amount (INR)

  INVALID     │    VALID RANGE           │  INVALID
  (below min) │  (1.00 to 100000.00)     │ (above max)
  ────────────┼──────────────────────────┼───────────
  -100  0.99  │ 1.00  50000  100000.00  │ 100000.01
        ^     │  ^                  ^    │  ^
        BVA   │  BVA               BVA  │  BVA
              │                         │
  EP: test    │ EP: test one from       │ EP: test
  one value   │ this partition           │ one value
```

```text
  Decision Table: Loan Approval
  ─────────────────────────────

  Condition       │ R1 │ R2 │ R3 │ R4 │ R5 │ R6
  ────────────────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────
  Income >= 50k   │ T  │ T  │ T  │ F  │ F  │ F
  Credit >= 700   │ T  │ T  │ F  │ T  │ F  │ F
  Age >= 21       │ T  │ F  │ T  │ T  │ T  │ F
  ────────────────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────┼────
  Action          │ OK │ NO │ NO │ NO │ NO │ NO

  State Transition: Loan Lifecycle
  ────────────────────────────────

  APPLIED ──approve──> APPROVED ──disburse──> DISBURSED
     │                    │                      │
     │──reject──> REJECTED │                     │
     │                    │──cancel──> CANCELLED  │
     X (cannot disburse)                    close─┘
                                               │
                                               ▼
                                            CLOSED
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Test-design techniques are how I get strong coverage from a small, justified set of cases instead of either testing exhaustively, which is impossible, or guessing randomly, which misses bugs. Equivalence partitioning is my starting point: I divide each input into classes the system treats the same and test one representative per class. Boundary value analysis then attacks the edges where off-by-one errors cluster. Decision tables handle logic where several conditions combine into an action, exposing missing rules. State transition testing covers an entity's lifecycle, both legal transitions and illegal ones. And pairwise testing tames the explosion when many independent parameters would otherwise produce thousands of combinations.

The key is that these are complementary. I partition to shrink the space, apply boundaries to the edges, use a decision table for combined conditions, use state transition for lifecycles, and use pairwise when parameters would explode.

At the National Bank of India this discipline paid off directly. For the transfer amount field I replaced a sprawling ad-hoc list of amounts with a tight partition-plus-boundary set and immediately caught a defect where the maximum used less-than instead of less-than-or-equal, so exactly one hundred thousand was wrongly rejected. For loan approval I built a decision table that exposed a missing rule for the borderline-age case the spec had not defined.

Being able to name each technique, say which feature it fits, and justify my case set as deliberate coverage rather than a random pile of examples is exactly what shows an interviewer I design tests like an engineer.

Remember one sentence: partition to shrink the space, boundary to find edge bugs, decision table for condition logic, state transition for lifecycles, and pairwise for parameter explosions.
